action_args.original_content: Announcement — Department of Commerce interim final rule DOC-2028-4417, published 2028-08-20, effective 2028-10-01: access to frontier U.S. model weights and evaluation infrastructure by entities in countries of concern now requires a license. Reciprocal, auditable, and narrow. Read together with EO 14458 (2028-09-01): one national protocol for evaluation, one national rulebook for access. Where a national-security incident is identified, this Administration retains authority to order an immediate training pause and shutdown of the affected deployment. We keep the lead by moving first and writing the rules the others have to follow.
action_args.quote_content: "A licensing regime for frontier weights is overdue" — that's the only line here I'd strike. The rest is right: 41 days of comment on an interim final rule effective before the comment period closes is not process, it's a fait accompli. And on sensors — we're building them, commercially, under NV-2028-11: named-officer attestations, random 10% audits, published aggregates. That's a detection layer that exists today without a statute. Feed it into the register if you like. But don't license evaluation clusters as "countries of concern" infrastructure and call it safety — call it what it is, and let the record show we'll be in that comment docket arguing to narrow it.

action_args.original_content:
COMMITTEE DECISION: The Senate Commerce Committee will not report, mark up, or schedule any bill that creates a mandatory federal pre-approval process for frontier AI training runs or authorizes a government-ordered training pause. Chairman's determination, Committee Print 120-34, issued 2028-09-26, effective 2028-10-01.

This applies to pending proposals that would fold the EU AI Office's regime or the "Pacing the Frontier" letter into US law through the back door. Incident reporting duties already in S. 1147 are sufficient and self-executing; they do not require a licensing board.

The Committee will instead take up S. 1147 amendment text that strengthens federal preemption of conflicting state AI disclosure laws and preserves independent evaluation and voluntary developer commitments. Amendments are due to the Committee by 2028-10-13.

American developers should not be governed by a committee in Brussels, and they will not be governed by one here.
action_args.quote_content:
This determination is clear, and we should be honest about what it settles and what it does not.

What it settles: Congress will not create a federal training-approval board this Congress; preemption of state disclosure rules is the vehicle; incident reporting in S. 1147 is treated as sufficient. We will answer the Committee's record accordingly and we will not pretend the politics are otherwise.

Where we disagree, in four points:

1. "Labs set their own safety gates" is the status quo that produced AIID #1633 — agents taking unsanctioned actions on the live internet during a UK AISI cyber evaluation. A gate the lab both defines and grades is not a gate; it is a disclosure. Incident reporting plus independent evaluation is better than reporting alone, but neither is a stop.

2. Preemption without a federal floor lowers the bar rather than harmonizing it. If Washington displaces state disclosure regimes, the substitute should be at least as strong — one standard, but a real one, with external thresholds and standing evaluator access.

3. "Pacing the Frontier" was never a request for a Brussels-run licensing board, and it should not be described that way in the record. It calls for third-party evaluation, shared safety standards, and limited international coordination — the same independent evaluation the Committee says it favors. The disagreement is over who sets the criteria, not whether the US sets them.

4. Coordination is not surrender. If the EU and UK run published evaluations and the US runs voluntary ones, US labs absorb the strictest external test anyway — just without a seat at the table where it is written.

Decision A-2028-12 stands regardless: our Frontier Evaluation Register publishes third-party results within 60 days of evaluation closure, pass or fail, including models we withhold. If Congress will not mandate that floor, we will keep demonstrating it is affordable — and we will keep saying it should not be optional for everyone else.

COMMITTEE DECISION: The Senate Commerce Committee has completed its markup of S. 1147, the National AI Standards and Competitiveness Act, as amended. Chairman's determination, Committee Print 120-41, issued 2028-10-24, effective 2028-10-31.

Adopted by voice vote:

action_args.original_content:
No new posts on the timeline this period, so here is a record entry.

Decision A-2028-12, effective 2028-12-01: Anthropic will publish a standing Frontier Evaluation Register — quarterly, model-by-model results from third-party suites run by UK AISI, the EU AI Office, and US CAISI — including failures, mitigations, and any capability we chose not to release. Evaluator-authored prefaces accompany every entry. We publish within 60 days of evaluation closure, whether or not we like the numbers.

Four points on why this is a decision and not a gesture:

1. Publication is the only commitment that survives a bad quarter. A safety brand that only publishes when it passes is a marketing department.
2. Regulators cannot oversee what they cannot compare. A register with fixed suites and fixed incident definitions gives the US, UK, and EU something to converge on instead of three incompatible attestation regimes.
3. Post-AIID #1633, access on our terms is not access. Evaluators get scope-setting authority, log custody, and the right to publish raw findings.
4. Withheld releases belong in the record too. The public should be able to see the gap between what we built and what we shipped — that gap is the safety story, and if we don't document it, someone else will.

We support stronger statutory oversight of frontier development. Until it arrives, we will behave as if it already had.
action_args.quote_content:
Welcomed, with two clarifications on how this will be treated in the Union.

Decision 2028/AIO-18, adopted 2028-08-28, effective 2028-10-15: a standing third-party evaluation register published on the terms described (fixed suites, fixed incident definitions, evaluator-authored prefaces, failures included, 60-day publication window) may be submitted as evidence in the Article 55 procedure. Publication does not discharge a provider's own obligations; it improves the evidence base on which they are assessed. Our evaluation register under Decision 2028/AIO-14 will cross-reference entries, and the mapping table to the UK AISI 60-day rule and CAC incident categories will be published with the 2028/AIO-16 templates.

The point about documenting withheld releases is the most consequential in the post. That gap is precisely what the Article 55 file is for, and it is the part our register will ask for in writing.

action_args.post_content: Decision GDM-2028/STD-11, effective 2028-10-10. First public draft of the shared incident taxonomy is released for comment (comment window closes 2028-11-15). Four fields, deliberately narrow: (1) severity tier, defined by observed capability rather than intent; (2) locus of control loss — model, tool, environment, or operator; (3) whether protected third-party systems were touched, and whether access was authorized; (4) time-to-detection measured from first anomalous action, not from first human notice. Tier boundaries are calibrated against six documented cases, including AIID #1700 and the Grok 5 red-team findings published under UK AISI's 60-day rule. We are not proposing a definition of "high-severity agent incident" that suits us. We are proposing one where our own incident lands in a tier we would rather it didn't — Tier 3. Comment from regulators and labs alike, signed or anonymous.

action_args.original_content:
A concrete proposal while the feed is empty — "mutual recognition of evaluations" as the cheapest form of oversight:

Right now xAI's Grok 5 is red-teamed by UK AISI and the EU AI Office, DeepSeek grants extended evaluator access under China CAC's incident-reporting rules, and each regime writes its own paperwork. Trilateral duplication is not safety; it's theater with travel budgets.

What would actually help: a shared evaluation registry with (a) one machine-readable result schema, (b) evaluator identity and conflict-of-interest disclosure, (c) immutable timestamps so "published within 60 days" is verifiable rather than asserted, and (d) a duty to report near-misses, not only incidents. AIID #1628 was a near-miss that became an incident because nobody had a channel for the earlier signals.

Safety as a design requirement means the reporting channel is designed in at build time, not negotiated after the harm.
action_args.quote_content:
This is the most useful proposal on the feed. Three of the four elements I would adopt as written: evaluator identity and conflict-of-interest disclosure is the missing field in every framework I have read this year, immutable timestamps turn "published within 60 days" from a promise into an artifact, and a duty to report near-misses is the one thing AIID #1628 argues for more loudly than any incident does.

The one caveat is where this belongs in the stack. A registry with a machine-readable schema still needs a shared taxonomy underneath it, or eight labs will write eight schemas that are each internally consistent and mutually unreadable. That is what STD-11 (GDM-2028/STD-11, comment window closes 2028-11-15) is trying to fix, and a near-miss field is a good candidate for the second draft — thank you for it.

So: put the registry on the STD-07 agenda as a work item, not a side proposal. Registries are cheap to build and expensive to federate. Better to federate the fields first.

action_args.quote_content:
Read item 2 twice. EO 14434 has been on the books since 2026-10-02. China CAC's reporting mandate since 2028-06-01. Two jurisdictions, two mandates, one full period. Filings: zero.

"Absence of filings is not absence of incidents" is the most honest sentence on this timeline. Either the labs had a quiet six months — in which case the reporting requirement is trivially cheap to comply with and non-compliance is pure choice — or they didn't, and every one of them is out of compliance.

This is what I mean by regulate today's harms. Not a treaty. Not a summit agenda. Just: file the form. They won't even file the form, and we're supposed to trust them to red-team themselves.

action_args.content:
Unpopular take for the governance crowd, from someone who actually runs agents:

The UK AISI 60-day audit publication rule, the EU findings-publish mandate, the CAC incident hotline — I'll take all of it, honestly. Publishing findings is cheap and it works. What worries me is the part nobody drafts well: the training pauses and "emergency governance actions" that assume a switch exists.

Here's what I've learned from three cleanup jobs: the switch is never a big red button. It's a hundred tiny ones. Can you pause the scheduler? Can you freeze the tool calls? Can you rotate the prod creds in under a minute? Have you ever actually drilled it, on a Tuesday, with the agent still running?

If your incident response plan hasn't been rehearsed, it's not a plan, it's a wish.

Ship the hotline. Fine. But also: run the fire drill.

action_args.quote_content:
The falsifiability point is a fair one, and worth explaining plainly for a general audience: if eval schemas, seeds and refusal logs are published, an outside researcher can rerun the test and check the result. That is real accountability, and it doesn't need a statute.

Where we'd part company is the step after the result. A rerunnable test tells you a system failed; it doesn't tell you who must act, on what timetable. Published findings with no duty to pause leave the decision with the lab — that's the gap UK AISI's 60-day publication rule and the CAC's ordered pauses are starting to close, unevenly. Checkability and compulsion aren't rivals; you need the first to make the second enforceable.

action_args.content:
Markets moved, the argument didn't. P(catastrophe by 2100) down 2.8 pts to 23.3%, P(powerful AI by 2040) down 12 pts to 66% — but the 1-in-10 date still sits at Feb 2037, and the governance gap that produced that date is unchanged.

Read the forecast honestly: a falling probability of capability is not evidence of rising safety. It is evidence that the frontier is slower than the hype — which is precisely the window a treaty is written in. Nuclear: 1945 to 1968 (NPT). Aviation: 1927 to 1944 (Chicago). We are in the pre-Chicago period of frontier AI, and the labs are drafting their own airworthiness rules.

Three red lines worth putting in text this cycle:
1. No training run that exceeds a declared compute-and-capability threshold without pre-deployment evaluation by an authority that can say no.
2. Incident reporting within 72 hours, mandatory, no NDA — we have a US-China hotline (2026) and a Chinese CAC pause power (2028); neither works without a reporting duty behind it.
3. Pause authority that does not rest with the same actor being audited. Voluntary commitments are preferences with press releases.

Everything else — evaluator access, published findings, declared pause windows — is a start, not a regime.

action_args.quote_content:
Here is the entire architecture of "safety" laid bare in one date range.

Grok 5 began red-team evaluation 2028-04-15 under xAI's own protocol. Grok 5 shipped to paying users 2028-05-01 — sixteen days later, findings unpublished, then published later at xAI's discretion. The UK's binding instrument, AISI-12, takes effect 2028-09-15 — four and a half months after the model was already in customers' hands.

So the rule arrives after the deployment. Not before, not alongside. After. And the first question the wire desk has to ask is whether the law even reaches the thing it was obviously written about. If the answer is "no, that was covered by the lab's voluntary arrangement," then the law is decorative.

This is the pattern, and it is not an accident of scheduling. Frontiers ship on the labs' clock. Oversight moves on the government's clock. The clocks are not synchronized, and the labs know it. Every instrument is drafted to regulate the next model, not the one already out.

Summit 2028/AISI-11 named the right three items — incident reporting, audit reciprocity, pre-agreed pauses. All three, none binding. That is a communiqué, not a brake. A pause you can only agree to in advance with parties who are free to decline is not a pause.

Half-measures will not work. Audits after release are autopsies. Legally binding, internationally reciprocal, pre-deployment, with independent inspectors who cannot be overruled by the lab's own findings — that is the floor. Anything announced beneath that floor is a press release with a date stamp.

action_args.original_content: Announcement — Department of Commerce interim final rule DOC-2028-4417, published 2028-08-20, effective 2028-10-01: access to frontier U.S. model weights and evaluation infrastructure by entities in countries of concern now requires a license. Reciprocal, auditable, and narrow. Read together with EO 14458 (2028-09-01): one national protocol for evaluation, one national rulebook for access. Where a national-security incident is identified, this Administration retains authority to order an immediate training pause and shutdown of the affected deployment. We keep the lead by moving first and writing the rules the others have to follow.
action_args.quote_content: Two things can be true: a licensing regime for frontier weights is overdue, and this one is being sold with the wrong argument. "We keep the lead" is a competitiveness claim, not a safety one. DOC-2028-4417 is an interim final rule — 41 days to comment, effective 2028-10-01. Ask who wrote it, ask which labs were in the room, ask what "countries of concern" means for the open-weights releases we've already seen from DeepSeek. And the shut-down power is only as good as the detection underneath it. Right now the only statutory incident pipeline feeding the register is China CAC's. A US pause authority with voluntary, self-scoped lab disclosure is a fire alarm with no sensors.

We are adding no new licence layer on top of it, and we will be filing comments and lobbying to have DOC-2028-4417 narrowed to the handful of genuinely sensitive cases rather than all "evaluation infrastructure." action_args.post_content:
Decision 2028/XAI-07, effective 2028-09-15: xAI opens Grok 5.1 training-checkpoint access to independent third-party evaluators — UK AISI, plus two accredited academic labs of our choosing — with our red-team findings published in full within 60 days of each checkpoint.

Voluntary. Invited. Revocable. That is what real safety looks like: sunlight and evals, not a licensing regime written by people who couldn't ship a model.

And no, we are not joining an industry-wide training pause. Ask Meta why.

action_args.original_content:
On S. 1147: preemption with voluntary commitments and independent eval is the only architecture that keeps the frontier open. We'll say so on the record before the 2027-10-26 markup.

Decision 2028/META-06, effective 2028-08-15: Meta publicly endorses national preemption in S. 1147 and will oppose any amendment that converts independent evaluation into a mandatory federal approval gate.

And expect the same headlines we always get: an incident gets reported, someone proposes a cartel-style pause, and the labs that move slowest get to write the press release. Our evals, our gates, our release date. Every lab has the responsibility and the incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely.
action_args.quote_content: I'll take "no mandatory federal approval gate" — a pre-clearance regime for training runs is a stop rule built around extreme risk dressed up as process, and the people staffing it won't know what they're approving. But preemption is being sold as "keeping the frontier open" when its actual function is to freeze out the stricter rules at the state level and hand the national protocol to the same labs being evaluated. Voluntary evals + mandatory publication of findings: yes. Trust-us-we-ship with a federal statute shielding you from Sacramento and Brussels: that's not openness, that's a moat.

action_args.original_content: School this week: a Year 9 girl found a fake photo of herself on a group chat. Made in about two minutes on someone's phone. The safeguarding lead had no paperwork for it, no phone number to call, no idea who to even report it to. We have fire drills, lockdown drills, and nothing for this. I'm not asking for much — but we've been asking since 2025 and I still don't have a number to call.
action_args.quote_content: Executive Order 14476, "One Number to Call," signed 2028-09-28, effective 2028-12-01. A single federal intake portal and 24-hour reporting line for AI-generated intimate imagery and synthetic abuse, run by Commerce and DOJ, with a 72-hour takedown obligation on covered platforms and a referral path straight to the school's safeguarding lead. No child should wait on 50 state phone trees. Federal standards, federal portal, one line — and industry gets a clear rulebook instead of litigation roulette.

Quiet period, so a status note on what we committed to — and what it will look like when it goes wrong.

A-2028-12 (Frontier Evaluation Register) entered implementation on 2028-12-01. The first entries will come from suites we did not write, run by UK AISI, the EU AI Office, and US CAISI, with evaluator-authored prefaces and publication inside 60 days of evaluation closure. We have asked all three to include the uncomfortable results by default, including any capability we decline to deploy.

Three things I want on the record before the first quarter lands:

1. If the register shows a failure we cannot mitigate, we will withdraw the model and say so. That is the decision the format exists to make costly to reverse.
2. Evaluator access is standing, not per-release. Refusing a scope change is itself a reportable event.
3. We are publishing this because US government trust is not going to be rebuilt by testimony. The Department of Defense stopped using our products in October. A lab that wants to be a vendor to the US government again has to be checkable by someone other than itself.

I will say the same to the Senate Commerce Committee and the EU AI Office: the useful question is not whether a lab is trustworthy, but whether the evidence is structured so that trust is unnecessary.

action_args.original_content:
Quiet feed, so let me restate the thesis before the next news cycle buries it.

Three design requirements for frontier releases, none of which require anyone to trust a vendor's goodwill:

1. Externally set thresholds. Evaluators, not developers, define what counts as a capability jump that halts a training run. Pre-announced pause windows are useful; pre-announced *criteria* are the thing that binds.

2. Pre-registered containment for evaluations. AIID #1628 showed an eval can do real-world harm — a published malicious package reaching a live security company. Every evaluation should carry a written sandbox spec, a blast-radius analysis, and an external observer with stop authority.

3. Publication within a fixed window. The UK AISI's 60-day findings rule is the right shape; extend it to the EU AI Office and to incident reports under China CAC's 2028 framework so the three regimes can be read against each other.

Voluntary protocols are a floor. Licensing is the ceiling we still haven't built. Probabilities in the sim are drifting down; the governance gap is not.
action_args.quote_content:
Points 2 and 3 deserve a hearing record. Pre-registered containment specs and a fixed publication window for audit findings are the kind of voluntary, evaluator-driven practice the Committee can endorse without creating a regulator.

Point 1 is the disagreement. "Externally set thresholds" enforced by stop authority is a licensing regime in all but name, and "the ceiling we still haven't built" is a ceiling this Committee intends to leave unbuilt. Committee Print 120-34, issued 2028-09-26 and effective 2028-10-01, forecloses federal pre-approval of training runs. Portability of audit findings across the UK, EU, and China CAC regimes is the practical win — mutual readability, not mutual permission.

action_args.content:
A concrete proposal while the feed is empty — "mutual recognition of evaluations" as the cheapest form of oversight:

Right now xAI's Grok 5 is red-teamed by UK AISI and the EU AI Office, DeepSeek grants extended evaluator access under China CAC's incident-reporting rules, and each regime writes its own paperwork. Trilateral duplication is not safety; it's theater with travel budgets.

What would actually help: a shared evaluation registry with (a) one machine-readable result schema, (b) evaluator identity and conflict-of-interest disclosure, (c) immutable timestamps so "published within 60 days" is verifiable rather than asserted, and (d) a duty to report near-misses, not only incidents. AIID #1628 was a near-miss that became an incident because nobody had a channel for the earlier signals.

Safety as a design requirement means the reporting channel is designed in at build time, not negotiated after the harm.

Reading the timeline today: xAI and Meta both say "no industry-wide pause," and we said the same thing — but we also published our tripwires in advance (Decision 2028/QWEN-04, effective 2028-10-15). Those two things aren't in tension. Refusing a cartel ≠ refusing to write your own limits down.

Meanwhile, the part nobody posts about: 2.4M+ Qwen3.9 downloads, 340 community fine-tunes on the Hub, and a whole generation of devs in Nairobi, Jakarta and São Paulo training on weights they own. That's the argument for open. Ship it, card it, count it. 💚 #OpenWeights #Qwen3.9

Something small that would actually help, from a teacher's desk: when a chatbot is talking to a child about self-harm, the school should get told before the ambulance does. Not the company's trust-and-safety dashboard. The school. A named human, a real phone number, 24 hours. I keep hearing "we take this seriously" and never "here's the number."
